text_fidelity_a:
TYR Socket Rockets 2.0 Racing Goggle As with other swedish goggles, these require precise adjustment to create good seal. It is critical to realize that these goggles sit in the eye socket, not the orbit. The key really is the proper adjustment of the nosepiece: it really needs to be tighter than appears. I recommend substituting bungee strap in place of the latex strap provided - it is easier to adjust and gives better tension. Actually, once properly adjusted, the soft frame feels quite comfortable and, even after wearing them for about 35 minutes, they cause less eye pain than the usual "orbit" goggles. Nonetheless, I would not recommend these for "occasional" and inexperienced swimmers. Be extremely careful not to get hit in the face while wearing these.
I agree that they fog up quickly. This seems to be a chronic problem: every goggles I've owned fog up. You can solve the problem by using a defogger (I love Cressi anti-fog spray which I use when I go scuba diving) or, just use a bit of spit and rub it in - cheap and effective. Some say rubbing toothpaste (yes!!) followed by gentle rinsing also works.
text_fidelity_b: TYR Socket Rockets 2.0 Racing Goggle

text_fidelity_a:
Stamina X Hyperextension Bench - Adjustable and Foldable Roman Chair with Smart Workout App for Home Workout - Up to 250 lbs Weight Capacity I needed something to work lower back at home, and have limited space. After reading lots of reviews, considering factors of space, budget and how users seemed to like various benches, I decided that The Stamina Hyper Bench was the way to go. It's been a week since my husband built the bench for me (thanks, honey!), which took under an hour, so let me give you my impressions.

First off, I'm 5' 3", so keep that in mind as you read. I found the bench is sturdy. It doesn't make creak, flex or make any noise when I use it, and all the feet stay firmly on the ground - no feeling whether doing back or abs that the bench might tip over. There was no damage to the paint, foam or upholstery, unlike a lot of other fitness equipment we've bought in the past. It's just a hint wobbly when not in use and rocking with your hand, but that could be our floors. Once you're on it and using it, the wobble is gone. And it had no plasticy, rubbery or chemical smell, which I appreciated. As far as value goes, it's much sturdier and easier to adjust than others I've seen at similar low price ranges.

One downside, and this only applies to people under 5' 5", is that with everything set as low as it will go, I'm a little short for the bench. It doesn't hit me at the hips but above, which isn't ideal but can be worked with. A minor downside is that doing ab crunches doesn't give much of a workout unless you're okay bending your back further back than flat, but I knew that would be the case in advance by watching the video.

BTW, this isn't showing as a verified purchase as I bought it from sports store that sent me a discount coupon.

To sum up, bench is sturdy and good quality. It arrived with no damage of any sort, has no smells, and was easy to assemble. Not ideal for those my height (5' 3"), and I wouldn't recommend it for anyone shorter, but it's a nice, useful bench and folds up nice and small to be put under a bed or in a closet. Overall for me this was a good purchase, an excellent value and good addition to my small home gym.
text_fidelity_b: Stamina X Hyperextension Bench - Adjustable and Foldable Roman Chair with Smart Workout App for Home Workout - Up to 250 lbs Weight Capacity

text_fidelity_a:
Eco Vessel Summit Discontinued 2014 Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle with Flip Straw (17-Ounce, Blue Glow) I really loved these bottles at first, so much so that I bought 8 of them. They keep my water very cold for a long, long time and I like the lids (I use them without the straws). I can hook them onto whatever I need to help me carry them, as well.

Unfortunately, my love affair with these bottles has ended all too soon. The first thing I noticed is that the paint started coming off. The red one is the worst. The paint is flaking off to the point that it would be better off if I pull the rest of it off to turn it silver instead of blotched red. But I could have lived with that.

What got me was when I started to fill one up only to discover that the plastic ring around the top of the bottle that you use to screw the lid in has split. It split completely down. There was nothing I could do. It had to either go back to the manufacturer or the trash. Since I'm a grad student, the last thing I have is extra time so I put it in the trash.

I started checking my other bottles and discovered that the plastic ring was put on at a tilt on some of the bottles (based on the amount of space under the ring not being uniform on all bottles).

Then I looked at my other bottles and noticed that the Hydro Flask's ring was metal, not plastic. I like those bottles just as much, but had to buy the straw lids separately. However, now that I see the flaw in the Eco Vessel bottles, I'm going to start replacing them with the Hydro Flask brand. Not only are they completely metal (except the lid, of course), but the finish does not show signs that it will flake off.

All in all, the plastic ring used to screw the lid onto the bottle is a fatal flaw for these bottles.

UPDATE: I added pictures showing the paint flaking off and the warped plastic at the top. I did not take pictures of the one that broke, but I thought showing one that's not broken yet, but clearly warped, might be helpful.
text_fidelity_b: Eco Vessel Summit Discontinued 2014 Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle with Flip Straw (17-Ounce, Blue Glow)

text_fidelity_a:
Leslie Sansone: Walk Away the Pounds for Abs: 3 Miles VHS This was my first-ever Leslie Sansone video, and I was surprised by how tough it was, especially given that I already exercise regularly and have even started a running program in the past month. Leslie uses four basic moves--march, side step, front kick, and knee lift--but varies the speed and execution of each movement to change the intensity. In addition, this workout uses Leslie's special weight belt for upper body toning work; I don't own the belt, so I substituted light (3 lb.) hand weights throughout the workout.

The workout begins with Leslie introducing the four basic moves, and in the warm-up phase, she gradually picks up the pace until you are moving along at a fairly good clip. At this point (about 10 minutes into the workout), she introduces use of the belt or weights for some basic upper body exercises, including overhead press and flies. For the middle part of the workout, or Mile 2, the weights are not used, as the pace increases considerably. Although the movements stayed the same, I sometimes found it a bit difficult to keep up with Leslie's quick movements. However, Leslie is extremely encouraging, frequently saying that it's okay to go at your own pace and not to follow her form exactly. For the first half of the last mile, the belt or weights are again used, repeating many of the previous exercises. The pace then slows down a bit to start bringing your heart rate back to normal, and finally, the last 2 minutes of the workout consists of cool-down stretches for a total of 44 minutes.

The only problem I had with this workout is the title, as I think it would have more appropriately been named WATP for Upper Body rather than Abs. Leslie does provide frequent reminders to concentrate on your abs and some of the moves (especially the knee lifts) do work the abdominal area, but the toning segments were more focused on the upper body in general. Overall, however, I found this to be an excellent cardio workout, and although the moves are repetitive, the time really does fly by. It is probably most appropriate for intermediate exercisers, but experienced beginners could manage by moving at a slower pace and skipping the weights.

Colisal Trekking Poles Collapsible Hiking Sticks for Women Men Walking Sticks Lightweight with EVA Foam Grip and Paired with Rubber Tips and Snow Basket Trekking Sticks 1 Pair 125cm I purchased a pair of trekking poles over 15 years ago and paid a lot of money for them. Although I do not use them a lot, I always had trouble with them, particularly getting on the snow/mud basket.

Therefore, when these became available, I wanted to see how they stacked up. These are not heavy duty like the expensive ones but they are still impressive, especially at the $31.99 price point.

They come collapsed as seen in the first photo. I did have some difficulty understanding how to get these to lock in place when fully assembled.  I had to pull down on the top of the pole until the little nub shown in photos three and four popped out. It sort of locks into place like an umbrella locks with the nub.

Once the pole is assembled, which is really quick to do once I figured out how to lock it, then it has to be adjusted to height. The clasps above the nub (photos three and four) opens to  relieve the tension on the telescoping pole in order to make the height adjustments.

All that is left to do is to cinch the wrist strap with enough room to hold on to the poles yet also allow one to release them. The strap locks into place with a plastic piece in the handle once the desired wrist width is reached.

I have no plans to collapse these poles again but that can be done if necessary. I got these for  my boyfriend and he loves them. He walked with them already. He just has to get use to using poles on a hike or walk.

Note that these poles come with a mud basket that can be screwed on (photo five) or it can be used without (photo six).

For the price, these are a good, lightweight alternative to the expensive ones and they are collapsible which makes them more portable than the other poles.
text_fidelity_b: Colisal Trekking Poles Collapsible Hiking Sticks for Women Men Walking Sticks Lightweight with EVA Foam Grip and Paired with Rubber Tips and Snow Basket Trekking Sticks 1 Pair 125cm

I had not considered reflective ankle and wrist bands before these, and so far I am happy with them.

Like the vests by the same company, these are a bright shade of neon greenish-yellow, a color that is very hard to miss when light hits it. These are designed for night visibility and they are excellent for this purpose.

I was able to attach them to the thick part of my calf but not to the upper part of my thigh - this is unrealistic placement but it gave me a good idea of how much these will stretch to accommodate. With two pairs in the package, if necessary they can all be attached together to make a waist band.

These are well made and should last for a long time. The elastic and velcro are of good quality and seem to be stitched together well. More importantly, the paint stripes do not rip or crack when the elastic is pulled tight which is the one concern I had. Because the paint also stretches, it should not peel which is a very good thing.

These are fine elastic reflective bands that should last for a long time and definitely increase visibility at night. Consider these if you need a reflective solution for nighttime running or cycling.

text_fidelity_a:
SUGARBEAR'S Smart Weighted Hula Hoop Corset Waist Trimmer Waist Trainer Fitness Workout Plus Size Pop It Fidget (One Size, Smart Weighted Hula Hoop) This is the first “smart” weighted hula hoop I’ve used, so I can’t compare it first-hand to others, but I can say that I found this one very difficult to use. First off, I feel the product description is misleading. It states “24 detachable parts” which is correct, but that doesn’t mean 24 separate sections as I think is the case with most of these types of hula hoops. After doing some reading about other models, it seems most have 24 sections meaning it’s possible to customize the waist band to best fit your body. With this hula hoop, there are only 2 large sections and 5 additional, smaller sections. The smaller sections are 5”, so there’s no adjusting by a just a couple of inches. For me, that didn’t work. With an extra section added, the hula hoop was too big and tended to move around too much on my waist and end up at an angle rather than parallel with the floor. With a section taken out, it was too tight. There was no middle ground to fit me. And as far as adding and removing sections, it’s not easy. The pieces are difficult to get into place, and even more difficult to open back up. The sections snap together, then there are white pins that hold them together (these count for some of the advertised 24 pieces). The pins are very difficult to put in and take out, especially when the hula hoop is around your waist. The weight on this hula hoop is just a flimsy plastic bottle with a screw top that you need to fill with water or sand. The bottle arrived partially crushed, it was difficult to pop it back into shape, and when I filled it with water and secured the cap, it still leaked sending occasional drops of water flying. It’s up to the user to tie a knot to secure the rope on the end of the weight meaning the possibility exists the knot comes loose and the weight sails across the room. Other hula hoops I looked at have a clip to attach the weight. The hula hoop has a counter that keeps track of revolutions which is nice, but again, it appears other brands have trackers that do more and provide more options to monitor your workout.
Overall, the hula hoop does work, but it’s not very customizable and not very user friendly.
text_fidelity_b: SUGARBEAR'S Smart Weighted Hula Hoop Corset Waist Trimmer Waist Trainer Fitness Workout Plus Size Pop It Fidget (One Size, Smart Weighted Hula Hoop)

text_fidelity_a:
Coleman 100 Quart Xtreme 5 Wheeled Cooler Having owned one of these for a few years I feel more than qualified to review this.

- To the people who say it doesn't work, first "temper" the cooler. That means you bring it inside, put cold items in it and let it sit. I temper mine for several days before use.
- Second, use block ice. I use the square ice cream containers from Wally-World. They pack nicely, stack nicely and are easy for me to get in my freezer to make the blocks. Barring that, keep the ice you guy in bags. The greater the ice mass, the less quickly it melts. I also use water bottles filled close to the top. I'll freeze them, cap them after they're frozen and put them in the cooler. You've a double use: ice and cold water when it melts.
- Third, make sure the products you put in the cooler start out cold. Again, the colder they are, the longer they'll stay cold.
- Fourth, don't expect anything in direct sunlight or on hot ground to stay cold. If you need, park this on a couple blocks of wood to get it off the ground and get air flow under it. Hot ground will eventually cause the cooler to become hot. Insulation doesn't care whether it's keeping cold things cold or hot things hot. If you get it hot, it'll start making things inside hot.
- Lastly, if you have water and still have ice, that COLD water makes a good conductor of cool temperatures. If you drain the water you're not doing yourself a favor. You should have your foods in ziplock bags for best protection.

I've used this cooler on an extended trip to the Sequoias from Eastern Washington State. This rode in the back of my pick up with only a tarp for shade. The trip south took three days (owing to stops at family and friends). No additional ice required. Once at the campground, still no ice required.
We were at the campground a week. After that week we did drain off excess and add more ice. The return trip was through Lake Tahoe on to Nevada, staying at Carson City for three days, over to Oregon - staying in Ontario, OR and then back home. Yup, most of the ice had melted, but the larger pieces kept the water cold.

If you take care of your cooler, it should take care of you. The handle is nice and wide with an easy grip. The wheels move nicely and everything feels comfortable when pulling it along.
text_fidelity_b: Coleman 100 Quart Xtreme 5 Wheeled Cooler

Marcy Folding Standard Weight Bench – Easy Storage MWB-20100, Incline I ordered this weight bench (March MWB-20100 Standard Bench) for my teenager and he loves it. I will first give you his comments and then end the review by giving my own.

A 14-year-old’s honest review:

In high school, I take weight training for PE. I have learned a lot but thought that some equipment at home would really help. So when my mom got this one, I was excited. This weight bench was very easy to put together. And because I couldn’t wait, I put it together myself instead of waiting for my father to get home. All I had to do was match the numbers to the pictures and the only tool I needed was a wrench. It was easy to assemble, only took me about 30 minutes to put together and I’m only 14. Don’t worry my dad did check my work when he got home. You can do a few different things with this bench. You can do the standard lifts or arm/bicep curls. I am 6’2, 159lbs and have really long arms, so it is a little close but is fine for me to use. By close, I am talking about the weight hooks. They are closer than the ones on the equipment I use at school. I also like that you can adjust the seats and back on the bench. This is great for when you work certain areas of the body. The cushions are comfortable and well padded with foam. Beware that this bench does not come with the bar or weights, but I had my mom to go to the local sports store and order some. I got a decent set for under $200. Regardless, I like this bench a lot. It allows me to build a little muscle without having to go to the gym at school. I deducted half a star for the closeness of the hooks.

Now what “mom” likes about this bench:

I liked the fact that he could put this together himself (I’m directionally challenged and his dad wasn’t at home), with very few tools. It occupies some of his time and gives him a productive outlet for teenage frustration and angst (smile). He can close himself in the room, play his music and pump away. And if I am so moved and want a light workout, this set isn’t so overwhelming or complicated that I am too intimidated to use it. BUT THE FEATURE THAT I LOVE AND THE ONE I THINK ALL MOMS WILL LOVE is the fact that by removing one of the pins, you can fold it vertically and it takes up little space. Meaning if you don’t have a basement, and I don’t….and choose to dedicate one room to exercise equipment, you won’t be overwhelmed by the size of it all. I have this bench in my extra bedroom, which is also a computer room. When company comes, or when I want to use the space for something else, I can release, pull up and store it. How fantastic is that?

And finally, as a consumer, this bench appears to be comparably priced with others on the market. When I priced bars and weights, I noticed that the local sports stores were selling the Marcy brand for comparably what Amazon was charging. Marcy is a brand known in the exercise equipment arena. The product appears to be well made and durable. For amateurs and young teens, this would be a decent purchase at under $250. I highly recommend it and give it 4.5 stars.
text_fidelity_b: Marcy Folding Standard Weight Bench – Easy Storage MWB-20100, Incline

- it's insanely light

1-3 BIKEHAND Bike Bicycle Floor Type Parking Rack Stand - for Mountain MTB & Road Bikes Indoor Outdoor Garage Storage The stand holds the bike upright and so it will not fall sideways.
Because it grips the front wheel so that it cannot turn right or left.

Nor slip backwards out.
And as you can see in the picture the bottom of the stand makes the bile roll back uphill,
and so gravity holds the bike from rolling backwards.

I do not agree with those who say this should work to hold a bike in the back of a pickup.
The bike could bounce out (overcome gravity) and roll backwards out.

In the garage, you will want a cover over the bike and stand to keep dust and dirt
out of the parts that have grease (the chain for instance).

Indoors you need a long pad (like an exercise pad to keep the dirty tires off the carpet.

Another (better for cleanliness) is a 'work stand' because these hold the bike in the air
and only the stand touches the floor (like a Park brand work stand). But these take about
15 seconds to load and unload the bike instead of 2 seconds like this Bikehand parking rack.
And work stands are much more expensive.
But a work stand hold bike so that you can do mechanical work on it, thus saving paying
hundreds to a bike shop for repacking bearings and such that you can do yourself with
a work stand and some specialized bike tools.

There are lots of other ways to go too, holders that mount to the wall or ceiling,
some have hoist ropes to raise and lower.

This stand is a very sensible and cheap solution, just keep in mind when the
bike is in a garage, then it needs a cover (cloth or plastic). Amazon sells
lots of these covers, they cost less than this stand.

Marvel Masterpieces Series 1 Sealed Trading Card Box 1992 My FAVORITE collection of cards!

I picked up a box of these cards back in '06 and they instantly became my favorite cards all-time.
Joe Jusko is the artist for the entire set and his work is off-the-charts-amazing.

You can do a Google "IMAGE" search for '92 Marvel Masterpieces and see the artwork...

This set (not this box - but the '92 MM set) includes 2 special sets in ADDITION to the 100 base cards.
Set 1: The Battle Spectra Cards 1-5D. These are all scenes of fights between various heroes & villians.
Set 2: The 'LOST' Cards 1-5. These are all individual females: Jubilee, Scarlet Witch, Typhoid Mary, Deathbird, and Feral

There are some other cards to this set that came as promos & prototypes, but I don't know enough about those to comment.

The reviewers who gave this set a low rating because the box was damaged or the cards are 'stuck together' should leave that as seller feedback - not on the item itself. There's no doubt this is a 5 STAR set - that's why you see boxes that originally retailed in '92 for around $15 now going for over $100. Collectors don't pay $100+ for junk sets. Crushed boxes and cards stuck together is a seller issue.
text_fidelity_b: Marvel Masterpieces Series 1 Sealed Trading Card Box 1992

This cooler is incredibly well-made and I'm thrilled that I got it! (I ended up buying everyone their favorite team's cooler in this same brand, and they were a huge hit over the holidays!)

The first great surprise when it arrived was that it is made by Coleman, with tags on it to prove it. Coleman doesn't make bad stuff, in fact, they have a long history of well-made products, so that was a really nice bonus.

On top of that, there are all kinds of quality extras built into it. For example, when you lift the lid, there is a mesh ice-pack holder built right into the top of it. On the outside of it, there are mesh holders on each side (I use them for napkins, straws, or nutrition bars). Then in the front there is a nice zippered compartment that you can securely stash a few things in. The zippers are high quality and the materials, inside and out, are high quality as well. The strap is wide, strong and adjustable. Another nice perk is that it has a little pad where the strap will go over the shoulder, which really makes carrying it much more comfortable. The cooler holds a lot, and really does a great job at keeping things nice and cold. I just put my ice packs in it with our bottles, sandwiches, etc., and we are good to go.

I also got one of these coolers for a friend who is disabled and likes to keep a cooler next to her bed. Well, she'd gotten fed up with coolers that didn't keep things cold for very long and she had switched to using a spaghetti pot (for real!) with ice packs in it, to keep her ginger ale chilled, for constant nausea. She said that with a few frozen ice packs in it, she actually can go two whole days without having to replace the ice packs. She also said it fits great on her scooter when she's on the go.

Made by Coleman, like I said, and with lots of nice features, this high quality cooler is a must-have and a great gift. Check out the same cooler with other team logos. Just make sure you get the one like this one from "TLG8," to get the high quality one I just described. Thanks for reading my review. Hope it helped someone.

I use this when I grill as well as when I visit state and national parks. There's nothing quite like being able to cook your lunch in the picnic area without all of the waiting for your coals to get hot.

Cons:

text_fidelity_a:
Nordic Walking Poles for Individuals 6’ 2” – 6’ 3” = 132.5cm SWIX of Norway. All 32 Lengths Coming Soon 1-Piece Non-Collapsible. #1 for Hiking, Trekking, Physical Therapy. My review is primarily geared towards people who are interested in learning the Nordic walking techniques and are looking for inexpensive, appropriate walking sticks. It is also a comparison of the sticks offered here and the so-called “crappy Chinese” anti-shock, telescoping sticks. I have purchased both and am including photos below.

I started Nordic walking about 3 or 4 years ago. At the time, I wasn’t sure that this was something I would continue to do and did not want to spend a small fortune on equipment that would, once again, end up unused in a closet. But I was having trouble walking even a short distance (100 ft. or so) without excruciating burning in my legs and back, so thought I needed to give this a shot. I sprang for the cheap sticks and boy, am I glad I did! Within a few weeks, I was walking a mile with very little discomfort. That distance might be laughable to some, but to me, it was a miracle!

But honestly, it had less to do with the type of sticks than it did with learning the proper technique. There are many videos available that demonstrate the technique and anyone interested should spend some time watching them. It is not difficult to learn. In fact once you get the rhythm it’s like riding a bike…you don’t forget how to do it.

As far as the poles go, I see little difference in them. Perhaps at a higher price difference there is, but it’s still more about learning the skills.

Cheap Chinese poles (the black ones in the photos): When I bought mine I made some modifications. The rubber tips that were included wore out quickly. I replaced those with the boot type of tip which has lasted all these years and many miles. The tips are deeply grooved like snow tires and they do pick up small pieces of sand. This will make them slip some on asphalt, but it’s fairly easy to flick a grain of sand out and continue your walk. I also replaced the sponge rubber grip just below the handle (because it tore easily) with some closed cell tubing that I found online. That wasn’t entirely necessary because you never or rarely grab the poles in that area. I should have just eliminated it altogether.

These poles are the twist lock telescoping type (not the clamp type), which is handy when you don’t know what length pole you need in the beginning. But once adjusted, it is a PITA to collapse or readjust them. They do have a scale on them that shows the length you’ve set them to, so if you get these, make a note or find some way of marking the length. I never collapse mine anymore, because I want to start walking immediately, not fiddle with adjustments. However, if you need to pack your walking sticks, and don’t mind messing with the twist locks, this is certainly a consideration when you buy. I have never had the twist locks fail or accidently collapse once snuggly hand tightened.

These poles also have the anti-shock springs. It makes them heavier and, yes, they make a rattling noise every time the pole hits the pavement. Their extra weight does makes their footfall more forceful. I see no advantage to the springs at this point, but I’ve heard that they are helpful when going down steep terrain. Can’t say, because most of my walking is on fairly level pavement. BUT, DO NOT let the noise stop you from buying if you don’t want to spend a lot of money in the beginning. Getting you walking again is far more important than any minor rattles.

The handle grips are very comfortable and include a strap for your hands to go up through. I found these straps were much more comfortable for me and more convenient to use. Just remember to insert your hand up from the bottom of the strap.

Overall, these poles have a bigger diameter than the “real” ones and are slightly heavier. However, I think the few added ounces actually give you a better upper body and arm workout than the lighter poles. So, to me, the extra weight could be advantageous. Cost for these poles was 14.95 for each pole (@29.90). The Leki replacement tips cost $17.31 with tax, and I highly recommend them. I’m not including the rubber grip which is not necessary, so my actual cost was $47.21 with tax.

Real Nordic walking sticks (blue in the photos): As noted above, these are somewhat lighter, thinner, nonadjustable, non-spring-loaded poles. It is important that you order the right length. They adjustable have glove like straps attached to the handle.

Personally, I’m not entirely pleased with these particular straps. As you will see in the photos, their design leaves something to be desired. I have circled the points where they irritate my hands. And here, I will have to make some kind of modification if I want to use these poles for an extended time. The gloves interfere with wearing my fitness watch and the binding on some corners should be more rounded instead of squared off. Strapping your hand in or out, by means of Velcro strips, is awkward; and should you need to let go of your poles if you fall, you’re out of luck. There is a means of length adjustment (by pulling upward on the handle top) which is lacking in the Chinese poles, but it doesn’t solve the rubbing issues, since the part which cradles your hand doesn’t change position. After I have used these poles more, I may try to fashion a strap comparable to the ones on the Chinese poles.

The handles themselves are thinner and (though you shouldn’t be clasping them tightly) may be more suited to smaller hands. I can’t say for sure, but they are still comfortable.

I have a gut feeling that the boot tips on these sticks will wear quickly, needing to be replaced often. However, they do not have the deep tread of the Leki replacement tips and do not pick up grains of rock or sand, so that is an advantage as far as sliding on pavement goes. I will most likely replace these stock tips with the Leki ones and just deal with the rocks.

The cost for these poles (before any changes I may make) is, at this writing, $77.45 including tax and/or shipping. I am, otherwise, perfectly satisfied with these “real” Nordic walking sticks. They are light, not noisy and do what they’re supposed to do.

Both poles need some slight modification, but their functions are identical. Once again, it’s about technique, not one type of pole compared to another. Please do not let any hype make your decision. It’s far more important that you get out there and start walking.
I'm awarding 5 stars to either kind of pole. Both work pretty much equally.
text_fidelity_b: Nordic Walking Poles for Individuals 6’ 2” – 6’ 3” = 132.5cm SWIX of Norway. All 32 Lengths Coming Soon 1-Piece Non-Collapsible. #1 for Hiking, Trekking, Physical Therapy.

text_fidelity_a:
M MAXIMUMCATCH Maxcatch 3-12wt Medium-Fast Action Premier Fly Fishing Rod-IM8 Carbon Blank for High Performance,with AA Cork Grip Hard Chromed Guides and Cordura Tube You see all of these reviews and they all start to sound the same, so I'll tell you where I'm coming from, my thoughts on the rod, and give my verdict.
I love fishing. There's nothing I'd rather do on the whole world. Nothing. You know what I mean... Lol! I've been fishing for decades, but have only been fly fishing for 3 years or so. I have several spinning rods in the $100-$200 range, and they are amazing. Unfortunately a $200 fly rod isn't the same as a $200 spinning rod. You can easily spend $3000 on a high end fly rod!

Well, I don't want to. I don't think it's necessary. But I've been fishing long enough that I can feel a great rod when I handle one. That's good, because I've seen lots of very expensive rods that were trash, and a few hidden gems that punched WAY above their weight. The Maxcatch Premiere line is one of those hidden gems. I picked this 3WT up just to check out, and after I effortlessly my fly 55' and landed it precisely where I wanted it. Over and over again. I mean it is so accurate that it's almost boring lol! And it's a $55 rod!

The blank is very sensitive, very light, very well finished and attractive, and the cork and dark chromed accents are beautiful. I'm surprised at how nice the cork is at this price point!

So I fish. A lot. I used to sell fishing equipment for a living, and I've handle a lot of gear. Is this Maxcatch a Loop or high end Sage? No. But it's also not $400-$900. However, I'd put this up against ANY Reddington, Fenwick, or lower end Sage any day and put money on the Maxcatch.

Get this rod. You'll be glad you did. You'll catch a ton of fish if you do your part, because this is a magnificent tool at an amazing price!

EDIT: I caught that monster 'Bow on the 4wt. Great fight! The rod was bent in half for 5 minutes, and held up great. And I felt every run, head shake, and dive. Great rods!

The trigger point roller doesn't have any give when putting your weight on it like other rollers, but the vibration helps counteract the stiffness of the product.

text_fidelity_a: Planet Bike K.O.K.O Aluminum Rear Rack, White I'm not the most mechanically inclined person in the world, but I have put a lot of stuff together over the years.  It probably took me nearly 2 hours to finally figure out how to best attach this bike rack to my bicycle.  I ordered the 29" rack because though I am female, I am very tall and have to ride a man's extra large framed bicycle.  The instructions that come with the rack are nearly useless, it says to attach it first to the bottom rear and then use the metal poles to attach it to the front.  If the bike brakes get in the way then use the longer poles that they include.  The longer poles were the worst and I quickly knew they wouldn't work.  There's a lot of wonkyness to it.....trying to figure out should it go this way or that, why isn't it lining up right, it's still hitting my brakes, what if I attach it to the lower holes instead of the higher ones in the back and on and on and on....  I almost decided to send it back.  I gave it one last try and assembled it from the top down and the Heavens smiled upon me and it finally got attached.  It doesn't come with a clip to hold anything on with so I guess I'll use bungee cords.  I just wanted it to carry my tennis bag and racquet when I go to the nearby courts.  It looks o.k. and seems well constructed.  And it matches my white metal basket on the front that's filled with tennis balls and my helmet's white so it all kind of goes together.
text_fidelity_b: Planet Bike K.O.K.O Aluminum Rear Rack, White

INSMEER Cooler Bag, Large Soft Sided Cooler Bags 65 Can Insulated Lunch Bag Leakproof Collapsible with Bottle Opener & Shoulder Strap, Lunch Box Cooler 48L for Camping Beach Picnic Travel It holds a lot and is more collapsible and lighter than a solid plastic cooler. There are bag coolers that have thicker walls than this, but this should be fine when transporting groceries home in the summer. I would not fill the entire product with cans and ice, like the marketing photo shows, since this would likely stress the seams too much. Use a solid plastic cooler for heavy items like that.

I would prefer if coolers had a plastic shelf on the bottom to keep the items away from melted water or spilled liquids that collect on the bottom. Most coolers do not have this feature. I have been using plastic liners that I took from my Tupperware produce storage containers.

The current price is $39. I see less expensive coolers that are probably just as good.

Features that some other coolers have are wheels for transporting heavy items, and some can be plugged into a car outlet or wall outlet for refrigeration. Other coolers collapse more when put into storage. This one is not designed to be collapsed, although it can be smooshed into a smaller shape when not in use. Good coolers can last many years, so you might want to invest in a high-quality one.

The quality is fantastic to the point where you could easily mistake this for an expensive, established brand. AND...even though Wild Man is or is not a good name, at least it makes sense, more or less, for a bike accessory.

Anyway, it seems like they got everything right, but just be advised that this is NOT the type of case where you can see your phone through the top, despite saying it's compatible with all these devices; that's just a way to add search terms, and I guess it's technically correct that those phones will fit in this bag.

While I haven't had this out in a downpour, it has what appear to be excellent quality, self-sealing zippers on the exterior that should be essentially waterproof as far as rain goes (likely not submersible). It's sort of a "shell" case in that it is semi-rigid, and the material has a checkered carbon fiber look to it, which is neat looking and will likely match a lot of fancier bikes, but will work with anything since it's basically black.

The three straps come large enough that I imagine they can be used with any bike, and can be adjusted down as necessary; I expect the cleanest and nicest installations will involve trimming the excess. The one strap is "across" the opening of the two sections, which would limit how far you can open it, except there is a piece of fabric inside artificially limiting how far you can open it, perhaps so that the former's limitation is not so obvious, but I suspect it will help keep you from dropping stuff out of the case while it is installed on the bike.

One side is a half-height net, and the other side is a full height zippered net, both of which offer some stretch, and are very much like a good piece of luggage.

This definitely adds a little bulk to your bike, and I'm not convinced everyone will want on for permanent storage (there are lots of other placement options to consider), but I can imagine that this goes quite far when doing multi-day riding with camping stops. The great thing is that it can be taken off and put back on quite easily, and as needed.

I am 5’9” and don’t fall off of it. I like that there are no rails on the side to run into. The price was perfect for my budget, and overall, I am very happy because I hate going to the gym, so, this is a great relatively inexpensive alternative.

text_fidelity_a:
Slendertone ReVive S5 Pro Muscle Conditioner & Stimulator - EMS Toning and TENS Therapy Device I have several of the TENS units which I do like very much, and I was curious to see how this compared since it's being marketed a bit differently than most TENS machines. First off the controls aren't as intuitive as they could be. That's not a huge problem, but having to refer to the manual almost every time I use the unit is kind of a pain. I'm used to being able to either figure the controls out on my own, or catching on as soon as I see the instructions the first time. The ReVive? Not so much. And the cautions are truly alarming. They made me wonder if I actually wanted to bother.

It's got a huge range of intensity, and on the lowest settings I frankly feel almost nothing. When I get up around 20, I start feeling a good level of intensity for me. I don't know if this is a problem with me or if the unit simply has a lot of fairly useless levels. However, once I found the sweet spot, the experience was pleasant, and by the end of the treatment, some of the soreness had left my shoulder. I tried it in several places on my body to test the purported strengthening effect, and I can't say I felt any increase in strength or performance. Perhaps I didn't use it long enough or often enough, or perhaps I'm not understanding the excessively complicated programs correctly. Either way, no points for the touted improved strength and performance benefit.

What I do have a big problem with is the price. The ReVive costs two-and-a-half to three times what my other units cost, and the cost of replacement pads is prohibitive compared to the other pads. I honestly don't know why this should be the case. I don't see it as being in any way superior to the less expensive units that I own. I get the same pain relief from them as I do from the ReVive at a price that doesn't transfer the pain to my bank account.

So honestly, I can say that it does fulfill the function of a TENS machine, though I remain skeptical about any other possible benefits. But all things being equal in that respect, the ReVive's cost and the cost of the pads is a problem I can't get past.
text_fidelity_b: Slendertone ReVive S5 Pro Muscle Conditioner & Stimulator - EMS Toning and TENS Therapy Device

With a sling style strap, I like the for the camera to hang on my right side with the lens dangling in front just above my hip joint.  This way, when I walk my leg isn't constantly hitting the lens barrel and making the camera bounce.  The way this strap is designed, as you shorten the sling loop, the plastic tensioning collar begins to come back around towards the front.  The two attachment points for the camera (I use only one) are forced toward one end of the pad attachment by the length tensioning collar.  So, as I shorten the sling loop, the pad rotates around so that most is on front.  When adjusted to my ideal length, only 3-4" of the shoulder pad is on my back, with the rest across my shoulder and in front.  Not ideal, but there is still enough padding for the strap to do it's job when I have the camera riding where I want it at my hip. text_fidelity_a:
Horizon Fitness EX-59 Elliptical Trainer I would actually give this a 4.5 likely. One thing that bothers me is that it's light enough that when I stand with my feet at the back of the treads and don't step too lightly, the front end lifts up a little bit. I just adjust my stride.
It's QUITE quiet. The only real noise is the friction of the runners at the base, unavoidable. Watching TV or listening to music easily drowns it out. The beeps mentioned by others IS also annoying. It's loud for no good reason. After the warranty is up, I might look into opening it up and putting something to adjust the level. I ran for a little over an hour today with my wife sitting only ~6 feet away watching TV and it didn't bother her at all.

I'm 5'9" and the height is fine. My setup isn't - best place to use is under a build (down) ceiling covering heating ducts, so it's pretty low. If I'm not careful, I bump my forehead. The fan blows more on my chest than neck or face.

I'm currently not in the greatest shape, but I generally use it at the 4th or 5th intensity level and move at the 6.8 (mph?) pace. I've used it 4 times for a total of about 4:30 hrs. My shoes were tight, so once I took them off. Bad idea. The treads were not good on my feet; the soles are still sore.

It fits in a small space much better than I expected. It can easily set almost right up next to a wall, unless you need access from either side.

I don't imagine I'll test out the speakers much, as if I'm running inside, I'll likely watch TV shows or movies, or do as I do when I run outdoors, listen to music with earbuds.

After a couple uses I noticed that I could hear a jingling sound. I remembered to check it after today's session and the bolt/nut on the front right tread was loosening. Glad I caught it. I tightened it up and will keep an eye on it.

So far I'm quite happy with choosing this elliptical. If I had the extra $200, I might have gone with the next model up, but I have no regrets on this purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Horizon Fitness EX-59 Elliptical Trainer
